introduction: The study aimed to test whether a 6-week digital literacy and digital wellbeing program was associated with more favorable pre-to-post changes in PIU, DSE and DGI than a wait-list control. A second aim tested whether post-intervention data were statistically consistent with a serial pathway from condition through DSE and DGI to PIU.
methodology: Two-arm pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with 206 adolescents aged 12–18 in Hubei Province, China, allocated by quota to an intervention group (n = 103) or a wait-list control group (n = 103). Delivered in person at a community center in March and April 2026. Measures were the SPIUT, the Internet Self-Efficacy subscale of the AIAS, and the short-form DGI. Analysis used 2 × 2 repeated-measures ANOVA and PROCESS Model 6 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples.
theory: The I-PACE model was used to inform the intervention logic. The DSE, DGI and PIU sequence is described as theory-informed, yet still a theoretical proposition.
results: Group × Time interactions were significant for PIU, DSE and DGI (DGI: F(1, 204) = 26.53, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.115). PIU decreased in both groups, more in the intervention group. DGI findings warrant caution: DGI dispersion increased markedly, particularly in the wait-list group, and its source cannot be determined. The standardized serial indirect effect was significant (β = −0.478); the direct effect on PIU was not significant.
discussion: The authors conclude that the program was associated with more favorable self-reported changes in PIU, DSE and DGI than a wait-list condition, and call the findings preliminary and hypothesis-generating. They name non-random allocation, a wait-list that did not control for attention or expectancy, and self-reported outcomes as limitations. They suggest digital literacy education may benefit from moving beyond one-time informational sessions.

introduction.q: The first aim was to examine whether adolescents who received the program showed more favorable pre-to-post changes in PIU, DSE, and DGI than adolescents in a wait-list control group.
The second aim was to examine whether the post-intervention data were statistically consistent with a theory-informed serial indirect association linking intervention condition, DSE, DGI, and PIU.

methodology.q: A two-arm, parallel-group quasi-experimental design with pretest and posttest assessments was employed.

theory.q: The Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) model was used to inform the overall intervention logic.
The present study further proposes that DSE and DGI may be connected in a theory-informed sequence rather than functioning only as separate predictors.
However, this sequence remains a theoretical proposition rather than an established causal mechanism.

discussion.q: This pretest-posttest quasi-experimental study found that participation in a 6-week multi-component digital literacy and digital wellbeing program was associated with more favorable self-reported changes in problematic Internet use, digital self-efficacy, and delay of gratification than a wait-list condition.
First, participants were not randomly assigned to conditions.
Second, the wait-list condition did not control for attention, expectancy, facilitator contact, or general self-monitoring.
Fourth, all primary outcomes were self-reported.
First, digital literacy education may benefit from moving beyond one-time informational sessions about the risks of excessive Internet use.
The findings are therefore preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

abstract_claims.q: Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for PIU, DSE, and DGI, indicating more favorable self-reported pre-to-post changes in the intervention group than in the wait-list control group.

The post-intervention data were statistically consistent with the hypothesized DSE → DGI → PIU indirect pathway; however, alternative-model analyses indicated that DGI showed the more consistent association with PIU across specifications.

These findings provide preliminary quasi-experimental evidence that participation in a multi-component digital literacy and digital wellbeing program is associated with healthier self-reported Internet use, stronger perceived digital competence, and greater delay of gratification.

Because participants were not randomly assigned and the mediators and outcome were measured concurrently at posttest, the indirect associations should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence of a causal or temporal sequence.

caveats.q: However, this sequence remains a theoretical proposition rather than an established causal mechanism.

When mediators and outcomes are measured at the same post-intervention wave, mediation analysis can examine whether the observed data are statistically consistent with the proposed ordering, but it cannot by itself establish definitive temporal or causal mediation.
DGI is conceptualized as a generalized regulatory tendency across various life domains (e.g., food, money, social interaction) rather than a digital-specific skill.
Because participants were not randomly assigned to conditions, the study should be interpreted as a quasi-experimental study rather than a randomized controlled trial.
This allocation procedure was intended to reduce imbalance in observable characteristics between groups; however, because allocation was not randomized, unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out.

Regarding assessor blinding, due to the logistical constraints of in-person delivery, research assistants supervising the posttests were aware of group allocation, so blind assessment was not achieved.
Nevertheless, the mediation analysis should be interpreted cautiously because the study was not originally powered specifically for detecting indirect effects.
Although no independent external fidelity rating was conducted, these procedures were used to improve implementation consistency.

These alternative specifications do not establish temporal priority between DSE and DGI.
The hypothesized DSE → DGI ordering should therefore be regarded as one theory-informed representation that requires longitudinal verification.

At the same time, the findings should be interpreted with appropriate caution.

However, because DSE, DGI, and PIU were measured at the same post-intervention wave, the mediation findings should be understood as evidence of statistical consistency with a theory-informed pathway, not as definitive evidence that changes in DSE temporally preceded changes in DGI or that DGI causally reduced PIU.
Importantly, the present findings do not prove that digital self-efficacy and delay of gratification operate in a fixed causal order.
Because digital literacy knowledge was not directly measured in this study, we cannot determine whether knowledge changed or whether such change contributed to the outcomes.

Social Cognitive Theory provides a rationale for considering DSE before self-regulatory behavior, but the present concurrent data cannot determine whether DSE preceded DGI, whether DGI preceded DSE, or whether they reflected overlapping processes.

Given that the intervention included direct training on these skills (Sessions 3 and 5), the observed changes in DGI may reflect both direct instructional effects and the hypothesized indirect effect through DSE.

However, because this study did not experimentally manipulate the sequence of curriculum components, this specific ordering remains a testable hypothesis rather than an established instructional principle.
However, scalability should not be assumed without further testing.
First, participants were not randomly assigned to conditions.

Although quota-based allocation improved comparability in age, gender, and baseline Internet-use duration, unmeasured differences in motivation, family supervision, personality, prior concern about Internet use, or scheduling availability may have influenced the findings.
Second, the wait-list condition did not control for attention, expectancy, facilitator contact, or general self-monitoring.
Active-control comparisons are needed to distinguish program-specific associations from these nonspecific influences.
Third, DSE, DGI, and PIU were measured concurrently at posttest.
The significant serial indirect association therefore does not establish that DSE changed before DGI or that DGI subsequently reduced PIU.
Fourth, all primary outcomes were self-reported.
The short posttest interval and absence of assessor blinding may have amplified this differential response reactivity.
Neither the decline in PIU in the wait-list group nor the significant Group × Time interactions can rule out this explanation.
Without device-based measures or independent informant reports, the relative contributions of behavioral change and intervention-related reporting change cannot be determined.
nevertheless, the source of the increased dispersion remains unexplained and warrants caution.
Sixth, digital literacy itself was not measured.
The study therefore cannot determine whether the program improved digital literacy per se or whether any such improvement accounted for the observed outcomes.
Seventh, the DGI measure assessed a generalized tendency across several life domains rather than digital-specific self-regulation.
Eighth, full attendance was not randomly determined; consequently, the per-protocol findings may reflect adherence-related selection and are descriptive only.
Ninth, recruitment from one Chinese province through online and community channels limits generalizability, and participating families may have been particularly interested in digital wellbeing.
Finally, only an immediate posttest was conducted, and the durability of the observed associations is unknown.
The findings are therefore preliminary and hypothesis-generating.
